parts.text:
Both answers, both built (`ca1e041`, Worker deployed):

**"Will it post an image?" — it does now, in both modes:**

1. **Link mode (default)** — the tweet is text + link, and X renders the card by scraping the page. The site *declared* `summary_large_image` but pointed `og:image` at the **global brand image** — so every shared post showed the same generic card. Fixed: image metas moved into `transformHead`, and each blog page now emits its **own banner** as `og:image`/`twitter:image` (the global entry had to go entirely — scrapers take the *first* `og:image`, so it would have shadowed the per-post ones). Verified in the built HTML. Bonus: this upgrades every share of every post on X, Slack, WhatsApp, LinkedIn, Discord — not just our poster. Ships with your site push.

2. **Content mode (the new alternative)** — a toggle in the composer: *"Content — article substance + banner uploaded natively."* Picking it re-prefills the draft from a **second template** (`{title}`, `{description}`, `{url}` — default `title / description / url`, editable in Socials → Settings alongside the link template), shows a **banner preview** in the composer, and on post the Worker fetches the post's banner PNG from ivue.dev and uploads it through X's v2 media endpoint — same OAuth 1.0a signer, since multipart fields stay out of the signature base string. Scheduled tweets carry the choice too and resolve the banner at run time.

The practical difference between the modes: a link-card tweet is one tap to the article but X's algorithm reportedly deprioritizes external links; a content tweet is native (image + substance, no card) with the URL as plain text — generally better reach, slightly worse click path. Having both lets you A/B them per post.

Evidence: 89 tests (mode prefill, banner URL derivation, template substitution incl. `{description}`), 30/30 E2E, gate PASS. Note the content mode's real send and media upload still activate with the X credentials — the whole pipeline behind them is tested against stubs and waiting.

parts.text: will content mode fill in all content from blog with code blocks and other images (from code samples that we generate for newlsetter)

Honest answer: **no — content mode today is description-deep, not article-deep**, and there's a hard platform ceiling worth understanding before deciding how far to push it:

**What it currently does:** prefills `{title} + {description} + {url}` and attaches the banner. That's it.

**What a tweet can physically hold:**
- **280 characters** (free tier) of *plain text* — no formatting, no code blocks, no headings. X Premium raises the length (25k), but it's still unformatted plain text; a code sample pasted in loses its indentation highlighting entirely. X's "Articles" long-form has no usable API.
- **Up to 4 images** per tweet.

**What we actually generate as images:** the banner, plus the **embed screenshots** (the interactive-demo PNGs made for emails). Note a subtlety: *code blocks are not images anywhere in our pipeline* — the newsletter renders code as Shiki-highlighted HTML, which email clients can display but X cannot. So "the code samples we generate for the newsletter" don't exist as attachable files today.

**The three realistic tiers, cheapest to heaviest:**

1. **Multi-image content mode** — attach up to 4 images: banner + the post's embed screenshots (we already commit those PNGs). One small extension to the uploader (`media_ids` is already an array). This is the best value-per-effort: a demo screenshot in the tweet *is* article substance.
2. **Code-blocks-as-images** — a build-time step rendering each post's Shiki blocks to PNGs (same local-Playwright pattern as banners/embeds). Doable, but it mints potentially hundreds of committed images across 34 posts, and most posts would still exceed the 4-image cap — you'd be choosing which blocks anyway.
3. **Thread mode** — the only way to get genuinely *full* content onto X: split the article into a chain of ≤280-char tweets, distribute the images across them, code blocks becoming attached images or "→ see the post" pointers. This is a real feature (build-time plain-text extraction into `blog-index.json`, a thread composer with per-tweet preview, `reply.in_reply_to_tweet_id` chaining in the poster) — a solid session of work, and threads do perform well for technical content.

**My recommendation:** build tier 1 now — content mode becomes "description + banner + up to 3 demo screenshots," which honestly covers what a reader can absorb in a feed — and treat thread mode as its own deliberate feature when you've got X credentials live and can see real engagement numbers to justify it. Tier 2 I'd skip: it fights the 4-image cap for marginal gain over a screenshot of the *running* demo.

parts.text: should i build linked in poster or you think newsletter + x should be enough to launch

Launch with newsletter + X. Don't build the LinkedIn poster now — and the reason isn't that LinkedIn is worthless, it's three practical things:

1. **The bottleneck is launching, not channels.** You have a complete distribution machine: drip newsletter with a ledger, X with link/content/thread modes, scheduling, images. Another poster is the classic pre-launch procrastination trap — infrastructure that *feels* like progress while the announcement doesn't happen. Ship the thing the machine exists to promote.

2. **LinkedIn's API is the worst of the three, maintenance-wise.** Unlike X's set-and-forget OAuth 1.0a tokens, LinkedIn's `w_member_social` tokens **expire every 60 days** and refresh tokens are gated behind partner-program approval — so the "automation" needs you to re-authenticate through a browser flow every two months, forever. Plus an app-review process to even start. For a channel where you might post twice a month, that's negative ROI versus the manual alternative: the composer already *writes* the post — copying it into LinkedIn by hand costs 30 seconds and reaches the same people. If it ever grates, a "Copy for LinkedIn" button on the composer is a 20-minute feature that captures 90% of the value with zero token upkeep.

3. **For the ivue audience, LinkedIn isn't even the next channel.** Vue/JS devs are on X, r/vuejs, Hacker News, Bluesky, and the Vue newsletters (Vue.js News, Weekly Vue). The highest-leverage launch moves are all *manual one-offs*: a Show HN, a r/vuejs post, submitting to the Vue newsletters. None of those want automation; they want one well-written post each.

So my launch sequence would be: **push** (everything's committed — dark emails, cards, the whole panel), do the **X developer-portal dance** and drop the four secrets in, post the first **thread** (the "One kilobyte is a feature" or "discovered, not invented" material is genuinely thread-shaped), and spend the LinkedIn-poster hours on the HN/Reddit posts instead — those two write-ups will move more numbers than any poster integration ever will. LinkedIn: paste the same text by hand, and revisit automation only if you find yourself doing that weekly.

so i have to make x dev account?

Yes — one-time, free, ~10 minutes. The exact path:

1. **Decide which account posts** — this matters first, because the app lives under the account that will tweet. Given the "Evgeny Kalashnikov" personal-brand direction and `@evgenykalash`, I'd post from your personal account (personal accounts massively outperform brand accounts for OSS reach anyway).
2. Go to **developer.x.com** logged in as that account → sign up for the **Free tier**. It asks a short "describe your use case" form — something like *"posting my own open-source project's blog announcements to my own account via an automated composer"* is exactly what the free tier is for. No payment, usually instant approval.
3. In the portal: **create a Project + App**, then in the app's **User authentication settings** set permissions to **Read and Write** (type: "Web App / Automated App or bot" is fine; callback URL can be anything valid like `https://ivue.dev` — we never use the browser flow).
4. **Keys & Tokens** tab → you need all four:
   - **API Key** and **API Key Secret** (the "consumer" pair)
   - **Access Token** and **Access Token Secret** (generate them *after* setting Read+Write — if you generated them before changing permissions, regenerate, or they'll be read-only)
5. From `newsletter/`:
   ```sh
   npx wrangler@4.120.1 secret put X_API_KEY
   npx wrangler@4.120.1 secret put X_API_SECRET
   npx wrangler@4.120.1 secret put X_ACCESS_TOKEN
   npx wrangler@4.120.1 secret put X_ACCESS_SECRET
   ```

That's it — no deploy needed. The Worker checks for the secrets per-request, so the moment the fourth one lands, the composer's "Credentials pending" flips to "Post to X", and Socials → Settings will show "configured — posting is live." These OAuth 1.0a tokens never expire; you do this once.

Free-tier budget: ~500 posts/month writes — a 10-tweet thread costs 10, so even a heavy launch week barely dents it.

The same runbook is printed in the dashboard at **Socials → Settings** whenever credentials are missing, so you can do it from there without remembering any of this.

That error means the app's **User authentication settings** don't have **OAuth 1.0a enabled** — the portal's setup flow defaults to OAuth 2.0 only, and our signer speaks 1.0a. Two-minute fix in the portal:

1. Your app → **Settings** tab → **User authentication settings** → **Edit** (or **Set up** if blank).
2. Enable **OAuth 1.0a** (there are separate toggles/sections for OAuth 2.0 and OAuth 1.0a — 2.0 can stay on or off, we don't care).
3. Under OAuth 1.0a: **App permissions → Read and Write**.
4. Fill the required URLs (they're mandatory but unused by us): Callback URI `https://ivue.dev`, Website URL `https://ivue.dev`. Save.
5. **Critical**: go back to **Keys and tokens** and look at your **Access Token and Secret** — it must now say **"Created with Read and Write permissions"**. Tokens minted *before* enabling OAuth 1.0a / Read-Write don't inherit the change — hit **Regenerate** on the Access Token pair.

If you regenerated, update the two lines in `newsletter/.env` (`X_ACCESS_TOKEN`, `X_ACCESS_SECRET`) and say "try again" — I'll re-push just those two the same way. The API Key pair doesn't change, so those two secrets stay valid.

(If the portal *also* offers regenerating the API Key/Secret during this, don't — only the access-token pair needs re-minting.)

Found it — and I owe you a correction: **my "free tier ~500 posts/month" claim was stale.** X [killed the free tier on February 6, 2026](https://postproxy.dev/blog/x-api-pricing-2026/) and replaced everything with **pay-per-use credits** — new accounts must [buy credits with a payment method on file before the first call](https://opentweet.io/how-to/x-api-pay-per-use-explained). Your "credits depleted" is simply a zero balance on a fresh account, not a misconfiguration — the OAuth setup you fought through is fine.

The actual prices are the good news:

- **$0.015 per post** — but **$0.20 per post containing a link** (X taxing traffic leaving the platform, which conveniently rewards our content/thread modes)
- $0.005 per read

Real-world math for your usage: a 10-tweet thread ≈ 9 × $0.015 + one link-bearing closer × $0.20 ≈ **$0.34 per thread**. A launch month with, say, 4 threads and 15 single posts lands around **$4–6**. **My recommendation: buy the smallest credit pack.** In the developer portal there should be a billing/credits page — add a card, load whatever the minimum is, and everything we built (posting, threads, images, scheduling) works end to end for pocket change. The cost-consciousness is even built in already: our content and thread modes put the link only in the closer, so most tweets bill at 1.5¢ not 20¢.

The fallback if you'd rather pay nothing: I can add a **"Copy" mode** to the composer — it formats exactly the same text/thread and you paste into X by hand (images too, by drag). Twenty minutes of work, zero credits, loses only scheduling. But given the machine is fully armed and threads cost a third of a dollar, I'd load $10 of credits and launch.

parts.text: we need site analytics what's good for our case? google analytcis or something newer?

Not Google Analytics — for one specific reason that dominates everything else: **your audience is developers, and developers run ad-blockers.** uBlock Origin's default lists block GA outright, so you'd be flying blind on 40–60% of exactly the traffic you care about (HN, Reddit, X referrals during launch). Add the ~90KB script weight and the GDPR cookie-banner obligations on a site whose brand is "1.1KB, no machinery," and GA4 is the wrong tool three ways.

What I'd actually do, in two steps:

**Now (before launch): Cloudflare Web Analytics.** You're already on Cloudflare — it's free, enabled from the dashboard in two minutes, cookieless (no consent banner), and the beacon is tiny. It gives you exactly what launch week needs: page views, **referrers** (watching the HN/Reddit/X waves roll in), top pages, countries, Core Web Vitals. Being first-party-ish it also survives ad-blockers better than GA. Its ceiling: no custom events, no funnels, shortish retention — it's a dashboard, not a product-analytics tool.

**If/when you want conversion tracking: PostHog.** You've already got PostHog connected to this workspace, and it's the right shape for the questions that matter after launch: *newsletter-signup conversion rate by referrer*, *which blog post converts readers to subscribers*, *did the X thread or the link tweet drive more signups*. Free tier is 1M events/month (you'll use a fraction), custom events are one `posthog.capture('newsletter_signup')` in the form we already own, and you can reverse-proxy it through a Worker route so ad-blockers don't eat it — a pattern we can set up in an afternoon since the Worker infrastructure is sitting right there.

The honorable mentions: **Plausible** is lovely and literally ships a ~1KB script (on-brand to the point of comedy), but it's $9/month for roughly what Cloudflare gives free plus events that PostHog gives free. And the artisanal option — hand-rolling a beacon into our own Worker + D1 with an Analytics tab in the admin panel — is *very* us and fully within reach, but it's real scope (bot filtering, referrer parsing, sessionization) at exactly the moment the right move is launching. Worth revisiting as a showcase feature later, not as launch infrastructure.

So: flip on Cloudflare Web Analytics today, wire `posthog.capture` on the newsletter signup when you want funnels, skip GA entirely. Want me to add the Cloudflare beacon snippet to the site head and the PostHog signup event to `NewsletterSignup.vue`?

Easy to tangle — the names are near-identical but they're three unrelated things:

- **Postmark** — the email delivery service. That's what we use, for one job only: actually sending the newsletter (and your signup pings). It knows nothing about your website traffic.
- **PostHog** — a completely different company: product analytics (events, funnels, session tracking). **We don't use it anywhere today** — it appeared in my answer only as a *suggestion* for conversion tracking. The reason I said "already connected": your Claude workspace has a PostHog connector available among its integrations, which suggested you'd at least brushed against it — but nothing in ivue, the site, or the Worker touches PostHog right now. If that connector was never something you set up deliberately, ignore it entirely.
- **Cloudflare Web Analytics** — part of Cloudflare (where the site and Worker already live), and my actual recommendation for now. Nothing to install conceptually: it's a toggle in your Cloudflare dashboard plus a small script tag, free, cookieless.

So the simple mental model of the current stack: **Cloudflare** hosts (site + Worker + D1), **Postmark** delivers email, and analytics is currently *nobody* — that's the gap. Fill it with Cloudflare's own analytics today; consider PostHog later only if you want signup-funnel analysis beyond what a traffic dashboard shows. No new vendors needed for launch.

No — don't move it, it's a false positive. The Cloudflare Web Analytics beacon token is **public by design**: its entire job is to be embedded in the HTML of every page you serve, so any visitor can read it in view-source regardless of where you store it in the repo. Putting it in `.env` would only obscure it in the source tree while the exact same string still ships in every built page — zero security gain, plus a build-time env-injection step for nothing.

The token isn't a credential: it can't read your analytics, access your Cloudflare account, or do anything except attribute pageview beacons to your site (and CF filters by hostname on their end). Same category as the two other "secrets" already in the repo — the PostHog project key (`phc_…`, PostHog explicitly documents it as a public client key) and the Turnstile **sitekey** (the secret counterpart, `TURNSTILE_SECRET`, correctly lives only in the Worker's secret store).

What to do with the alert: in the GitGuardian dashboard, mark the incident as **"False positive"** (or "Ignore — low risk"), so it stops flagging. GitGuardian pattern-matches hex strings and can't tell a public beacon token from a real key.

The actual secrets in this project — Postmark token, admin secret, Turnstile secret, the four X OAuth keys — are all only in Wrangler's secret store and `newsletter/.env` (gitignored, never read into context), so the repo hygiene is already right.

route. It shows lists/status, full send history, and "Coming up": every
catalog post the address hasn't received, in drip order, each with its
projected send time (`GET /admin/subscriber` unrolls the drip's own
rule — one email per cadence from the last send — to the end of the
archive). Unsubscribed addresses show a "pipeline paused" banner.

## Why the 2nd drip email was `computed-is-a-cache`

Not a bug — an accident of git history. Previewable in the dashboard like any post.
